units.name: Functions & Their Graphs

concepts.intro: A function f assigns exactly one output f(x) to each input x. Function notation f(x) replaces 'y' and lets you name and evaluate relations precisely.
b: f(x) is read 'f of x' — NOT f times x
To evaluate f(3), substitute 3 for every x in the rule: $f(x)=2x²−1$ → $f(3)=2(9)−1=17$
Vertical Line Test: a graph represents a function iff every vertical line crosses it at most once
Composite functions: ($f∘g)(x)=f(g(x$)) — evaluate the INSIDE function first
Example: $f(x)=x+2, g(x)=x². (f∘g)(3)=f(9)=11. (g∘f)(3)=g(5)=25$ — order matters!
Difference quotient: [f(x+h)−f(x)]/h, the building block for average rate of change and derivatives

concepts.intro: Domain $=$ all valid x-inputs; range $=$ all resulting y-outputs. Restrictions come from division by zero, even roots of negatives, and logs of non-positives.
b: Rational functions: exclude x-values that make the denominator 0 (e.g., $f(x)=1/(x−3$): domain is x≠3)
Even-root functions: the radicand must be ≥0 (e.g., $f(x)=√(x−4$): domain is x≥4)
Polynomial functions: domain is always all real numbers (−∞,∞)
Range is found from the graph's minimum/maximum behavior (e.g., $y=x²$ has range y≥0)
Interval notation: use parentheses for excluded endpoints, brackets for included endpoints
Domain of a sum/product/quotient of functions $=$ intersection of each piece's domain (and denominator ≠0 for quotients)

concepts.intro: Given a parent function f(x), transformations shift, stretch, compress, or reflect the graph. Changes INSIDE the parentheses affect x (opposite/counterintuitive direction); changes OUTSIDE affect y (intuitive direction).
b: f(x)+k: shifts UP k units (k>0) | f(x)−k: shifts DOWN k units
f(x−h): shifts RIGHT h units | f(x+h): shifts LEFT h units (opposite of the sign!)
a·f(x): vertical stretch if |a|>1, vertical compression if 0<|a|<1
f(bx): horizontal compression if |b|>1, horizontal stretch if 0<|b|<1
−f(x): reflects over the x-axis | f(−x): reflects over the y-axis
Order of operations for combined transformations: horizontal shift/stretch first (inside), then vertical stretch, then vertical shift (outside)

concepts.intro: Symmetry tests reveal structure that simplifies graphing and algebra (useful later for trig identities and integration).
b: Even function: $f(−x)=f(x$) for all x — graph is symmetric about the y-axis (e.g., $f(x)=x², f(x)=cos$ x)
Odd function: $f(−x)=−f(x$) for all x — graph has 180° rotational symmetry about the origin (e.g., $f(x)=x³, f(x)=sin$ x)
To test algebraically: plug −x into f(x), simplify, and compare to f(x) and −f(x)
A function can be neither even nor odd (most functions), but cannot be both unless $f(x)=0$ for all x
Sum of two even functions is even; sum of two odd functions is odd; product of two odd functions is even

concepts.intro: A piecewise function uses different formulas over different intervals of the domain. Evaluate by first identifying which interval the input falls into.
b: Notation: $f(x)={rule₁$ if x<a; rule₂ if x≥a} — check the given x against each interval's boundary
Example: $f(x)={x+3$ if x<2; x² if x≥2}. $f(2)=2²=4$ (use second rule since 2≥2); $f(−1)=−1+3=2$
Graph each piece only over its stated domain; use open circles for excluded endpoints, closed circles for included
Step functions (e.g., the greatest integer/floor function ⌊x⌋) are a special piecewise case with constant horizontal segments
Continuity at a breakpoint requires the two pieces to meet at the same y-value there

traps: f(x+2) is NOT f(x)+2 — you substitute (x+2) for x everywhere it appears, don't just add 2 to the output.
Horizontal shifts move opposite the sign inside parentheses: f(x−3) shifts RIGHT, not left.
An even function is symmetric about the y-axis; an odd function is symmetric about the ORIGIN, not the x-axis.
In a piecewise function, always check boundary inequalities (< vs ≤) carefully — using the wrong piece gives the wrong value.

units.name: Polynomial & Rational Functions

concepts.intro: The leading term (highest-degree term) determines what happens to y as x→±∞.
b: Odd degree, positive leading coefficient: falls left, rises right (like $y=x³$)
Odd degree, negative leading coefficient: rises left, falls right (like $y=−x³$)
Even degree, positive leading coefficient: rises left and right (like $y=x²$)
Even degree, negative leading coefficient: falls left and right (like $y=−x²$)
Degree $=$ maximum number of real zeros (counting multiplicity) and one less than the max number of turning points
Example: $f(x)=−2x⁵+3x²−1$ has odd degree (5) and negative leading coefficient → rises left, falls right

concepts.intro: Zeros (roots) of a polynomial are the x-values where $f(x)=0$ — where the graph crosses or touches the x-axis.
b: Factor completely, set each factor to 0, solve for x (zero product property)
Multiplicity 1 (odd, simple): graph CROSSES the x-axis at that zero
Multiplicity 2 (even): graph TOUCHES the x-axis and turns back (bounces)
Multiplicity 3 (odd, ≥3): graph crosses but flattens (inflects) at that zero
Example: $f(x)=x³−4x =$ x(x−2)(x+2) → zeros at $x=0,2,−2$, each multiplicity 1, all crossings
Difference of squares: $a²−b²=(a−b)(a+b$); sum/difference of cubes: $a³±b³=(a±b)(a²∓ab+b²$)

concepts.intro: The Rational Root Theorem narrows down candidate rational zeros of a polynomial before testing them.
b: Possible rational roots $=$ ±(factors of constant term)/(factors of leading coefficient)
Example: $2x³−3x²−11x+6=0$ → $constant=6$ (factors 1,2,3,6), $leading=2$ (factors 1,2) → candidates ±1,2,3,6,1/2,3/2
Test candidates using synthetic division; a remainder of 0 confirms a root and gives the depressed (reduced) polynomial
Synthetic division steps: bring down leading coefficient, multiply by the root, add to next coefficient, repeat
Example: dividing 2x³−3x²−11x+6 by (x−3) using synthetic division with root 3 gives 2x²+3x−2 remainder 0, confirming $x=3$ is a root
Once reduced to a quadratic, use factoring or the quadratic formula to find remaining roots

concepts.intro: A rational function is a ratio of two polynomials, $f(x)=p(x)/q(x$). Its graph is shaped by vertical, horizontal, and sometimes slant asymptotes.
b: Vertical asymptote: at x-values where the denominator $=$ 0 AND the numerator ≠ 0 there (a hole occurs if both are 0 after cancelling common factors)
Horizontal asymptote (compare degrees of numerator n and denominator m): if n<m, $y=0$; if $n=m, y=(ratio$ of leading coefficients); if n>m, no horizontal asymptote
Slant (oblique) asymptote exists when $n=m+1$ exactly one degree higher — found via polynomial long division, ignoring the remainder
Example: $f(x)=(x²−1)/(x−1$) simplifies to x+1 with a HOLE at $x=1$ (not a vertical asymptote) since (x−1) cancels
Example: $f(x)=(3x²+1)/(x²−4$) has horizontal asymptote $y=3$ (equal degrees, ratio of leading coefficients 3/1) and vertical asymptotes at $x=±2$

concepts.intro: Clear denominators by multiplying through by the LCD, but always check for extraneous solutions that make an original denominator zero.
b: Multiply every term by the LCD to eliminate fractions, then solve the resulting polynomial equation
Always check solutions back in the ORIGINAL equation — any value making a denominator 0 must be rejected (extraneous)
For rational inequalities: move everything to one side, find critical values (zeros and undefined points), test each interval on a sign chart
Example: solve (x−1)/(x+2)≥0 → critical values $x=1, x=−2$ (excluded, open circle); test intervals → solution x<−2 or x≥1

traps: A 'hole' occurs when a factor cancels from both numerator and denominator — it is NOT a vertical asymptote.
Always check rational-equation solutions in the original equation; a value that zeroes a denominator must be rejected.
Even multiplicity means the graph BOUNCES off the x-axis; odd multiplicity means it CROSSES.
Comparing degrees for horizontal asymptotes: if the numerator's degree is strictly greater, there is NO horizontal asymptote (there may be a slant one instead).
fms: Rational Root candidates $=$ ±(factors of constant)/(factors of leading coeff)

units.name: Exponential & Logarithmic Functions

concepts.intro: Exponential functions model quantities that grow or shrink by a constant PERCENT rate over equal time intervals: $A(t)=A₀(1+r)^t$ (growth) or $A(t)=A₀(1−r)^t$ (decay).
b: A₀ $=$ initial amount, r $=$ rate as a decimal, t $=$ number of time periods, $b=(1+r$) or (1−r) is the growth/decay factor
If b>1 the function models growth; if 0<b<1 it models decay
Example: population growing 5%/year from 2000: $A(t)=2000(1.05)^t$ → after 10 years $A(10)=2000(1.05)¹⁰≈3257.8$
Continuous growth/decay uses $A(t)=A₀e^(rt$) where e≈2.71828 (r>0 growth, r<0 decay)
Half-life problems: $A(t)=A₀(1/2)^(t/h$) where h is the half-life
Compound interest: $A=P(1+r/n)^(nt$); continuously compounded: $A=Pe^(rt$)

concepts.intro: These rules let you simplify and manipulate expressions with the same base before solving exponential equations.
b: Product rule: $bᵐ·bⁿ=bᵐ⁺ⁿ$ | Quotient rule: $bᵐ/bⁿ=bᵐ⁻ⁿ$
Power rule: ($bᵐ)ⁿ=bᵐⁿ$ | Power of a product: ($ab)ⁿ=aⁿbⁿ$
Zero exponent: $b⁰=1$ (b≠0) | Negative exponent: $b⁻ⁿ=1/bⁿ$
Rational (fractional) exponent: $b^(m/n)=ⁿ√(bᵐ)=(ⁿ√b)ᵐ$
To solve exponential equations with matching bases: set exponents equal once bases match (e.g., $2^(x+1)=8$ → $2^(x+1)=2³$ → $x+1=3$ → $x=2$)

concepts.intro: A logarithm is the inverse operation of exponentiation: $log_b(x)=y$ means $bʸ=x$. Logs answer 'to what power must b be raised to get x?'
b: Product rule: $log_b(MN)=log_b(M)+log_b(N$)
Quotient rule: $log_b(M/N)=log_b(M)−log_b(N$)
Power rule: $log_b(Mᵏ)=k·log_b(M$)
$log_b(1)=0$ always (since $b⁰=1); log_b(b)=1$ always (since $b¹=b$)
Change of base formula: $log_b(x)=ln(x)/ln(b)=log(x)/log(b$) — needed for bases other than 10 or e on a calculator

concepts.intro: Use inverse operations — take logs to bring down exponents, or exponentiate to remove logs — and always check for extraneous solutions in log equations.
b: To solve $bˣ=k$ (unlike bases): take ln or log of both sides → $x=ln(k)/ln(b$)
To solve $log_b(x)=k$: rewrite in exponential form $x=bᵏ$
Example: $log₂(x)=5$ → $x=2⁵=32$
When both sides are logs with the same base: $log_b(A)=log_b(B$) ⟹ $A=B$ (then check domain — argument must stay positive)
Extraneous solutions: after solving a log equation, reject any solution that makes an argument of a log ≤0 in the ORIGINAL equation

concepts.intro: The natural logarithm $ln(x)=log_e(x$) uses base e≈2.71828..., the base for continuous growth/decay and calculus.
b: ln(x) and eˣ are inverse functions: $ln(eˣ)=x$ and $e^(ln x)=x$
Solve $eˣ=k$ by taking ln of both sides: $x=ln(k$)
Solve $ln(x)=k$ by exponentiating: $x=eᵏ$
Continuous compounding/growth: $A=Pe^(rt$) — appears in population models, radioactive decay, and continuously compounded interest

traps: log(A+B) is NOT log(A)+log(B) — there is no log rule for sums/differences inside a single log.
$log_b(x$) is only defined for x>0 — always check the domain restriction before finalizing a log-equation solution.
(1+r) is used for growth, (1−r) for decay — mixing up the sign of r gives the wrong model entirely.
Change of base requires dividing (ln x)/(ln b), not (ln b)/(ln x) — order matters.

units.name: Trigonometric Functions

concepts.intro: The unit circle has radius 1, centered at the origin. For an angle $θ$ measured from the positive x-axis, the terminal point is (cos $θ$, sin $θ$).
b: cos $θ =$ x-coordinate, sin $θ =$ y-coordinate of the point where the terminal ray meets the circle
tan $θ =$ sin $θ$ / cos $θ =$ y/x (undefined when cos $θ=0$, i.e., $θ=90°,270°$)
Quadrant signs (ASTC, 'All Students Take Calculus'): QI all positive, QII sine positive, QIII tangent positive, QIV cosine positive
Key points to memorize: (1,0) at 0°, (0,1) at 90°, (−1,0) at 180°, (0,−1) at 270°
The unit circle repeats every 360° ($2π$ radians) — this is why trig functions are periodic

concepts.intro: Radians measure angles as arc length divided by radius; a full circle is $2π$ radians $=$ 360°.
b: Conversion: radians $=$ degrees × ($π/180$) | degrees $=$ radians × ($180/π$)
Example: convert 150° to radians: $150×(π/180)=5π/6$
Example: convert $7π/4$ rad to degrees: ($7π/4)×(180/π)=315°$
Arc length formula: $s=rθ (θ$ MUST be in radians)
Angular/linear speed problems use $s=rθ$ and $v=s/t$ or $ω=θ/t (ω$ in rad/time)

concepts.l: Graphs of sine, cosine, and tangent
concepts.intro: $y=A$ sin(Bx−C)+D and $y=A$ cos(Bx−C)+D describe transformed sinusoids; $y=tan$ x has a different shape with vertical asymptotes.
b: Amplitude $=$ |A| (half the distance between max and min); period $= 2π/|B|$
Phase shift $=$ C/B (shift right if positive); vertical shift $=$ D (midline $y=D$)
$y=sin$ x: starts at midline going up, zeros at $0,π,2π$, max at $π/2$, min at $3π/2$
$y=cos$ x: starts at max, zeros at $π/2,3π/2$, min at $π$
$y=tan$ x has period $π$ (not $2π$) and vertical asymptotes at $x=π/2+kπ$; no amplitude (unbounded range)
Example: $y=3sin(2x)+1$ has amplitude 3, period $2π/2=π$, midline $y=1$, no phase shift

concepts.intro: A reference angle is the acute angle (0°–90°) between the terminal side and the x-axis — used to find exact trig values in any quadrant.
b: QI: reference angle $= θ$ itself
QII: reference angle $= 180°−θ$ (or $π−θ$)
QIII: reference angle $= θ−180°$ (or $θ−π$)
QIV: reference angle $= 360°−θ$ (or $2π−θ$)
Find the trig value of the reference angle, then apply the correct sign for the original quadrant (ASTC)
Example: sin(210°): QIII, reference $angle=210−180=30°, \sin(30°)=1/2$, QIII sine is negative → $\sin(210°)=−1/2$

concepts.intro: Exact values for 0°,30°,45°,60°,90° (and their radian equivalents) must be memorized — they recur constantly in identities and equations.
b: $90°(π/2): sin=1, cos=0, tan=undefined$
Memory trick: sin values at 0°,30°,45°,60°,90° follow √0/2,√1/2,√2/2,√3/2,√4/2 (simplify each); cos is the reverse order

traps: Arc length $s=rθ$ requires $θ$ in RADIANS — using degrees gives a wrong answer without a conversion.
tan $θ$ is undefined wherever cos $θ=0$ (90°,270°) — these are vertical asymptotes on the tangent graph, not zeros.
The reference angle is always POSITIVE and between 0° and 90° — never use the original angle's sign for it.
Period of tan x is $π$, not $2π$ like sine and cosine — don't apply the sine/cosine period formula to tangent.

units.name: Trigonometric Identities & Equations

concepts.intro: Derived directly from $x²+y²=r²=1$ on the unit circle, these are the most fundamental trig identities.
b: $sin²θ+cos²θ=1$ (the core identity — memorize this one first)
Divide by $cos²θ: 1+tan²θ=sec²θ$
Divide by $sin²θ: 1+cot²θ=csc²θ$
Rearranged forms are useful for simplifying: $sin²θ=1−cos²θ, cos²θ=1−sin²θ$
Example: simplify $sin²θ/(1−cos θ$) using $1−cos²θ=(1−\cosθ)(1+\cosθ): sin²θ/(1−\cosθ)=(1−\cosθ)(1+\cosθ)/(1−\cosθ)=1+\cosθ$

concepts.intro: These formulas expand trig functions of a sum or difference of two angles — used to find exact values of non-special angles like 15° or 75°.
b: $\sin(A±B)=sin$ A cos B ± cos A sin B
$\cos(A±B)=cos$ A cos B ∓ sin A sin B (note the sign FLIPS for cosine)
$\tan(A±B)=(tan$ A ± tan B)/(1 ∓ tan A tan B)
Cofunction identities follow from these: $\sin(90°−θ)=cos θ, \cos(90°−θ)=sin θ$

concepts.intro: Double-angle formulas express trig functions of $2θ$ in terms of single $θ$ — derived by setting $A=B=θ$ in the sum formulas.
b: $\sin(2θ)=2$ sin $θ$ cos $θ$
$\cos(2θ)=cos²θ−sin²θ = 2cos²θ−1 = 1−2sin²θ$ (three equivalent forms — pick based on what's given)
$\tan(2θ)=2tanθ/(1−tan²θ$)
Example: if $\sinθ=3/5$ and $θ$ in QI ($\cosθ=4/5$), then $\sin(2θ)=2(3/5)(4/5)=24/25$
Half-angle formulas (derived from double-angle, less common but related): $\sin(θ/2)=±√[(1−\cosθ)/2], \cos(θ/2)=±√[(1+\cosθ)/2]$

concepts.intro: Solve for $θ$ using algebra and identities, then use the unit circle/reference angles to find ALL solutions in the given interval, remembering periodicity.
b: Isolate the trig function first, then find the reference angle from its exact value
Find every solution in $[0,2π$) or [0°,360°) by applying the correct quadrant signs (ASTC), then add multiples of the period for a general solution ($+2πk$ or +360°k)
Example: solve $2sinθ−1=0$ on $[0,2π): \sinθ=1/2$ → reference angle $π/6$ → sine positive in QI,QII → $θ=π/6, 5π/6$
For quadratics in a trig function (e.g., $2sin²θ−\sinθ−1=0$), factor like a normal quadratic: ($2sinθ+1)(\sinθ−1)=0$ → $\sinθ=−1/2$ or $\sinθ=1$
When an equation has multiple trig functions, use identities (Pythagorean, double-angle) to rewrite everything in terms of ONE function before solving

traps: cos(A+B) ≠ cos A + cos B — you must use the full sum formula, not distribute like multiplication.
There are THREE equivalent forms of $\cos(2θ$) — pick the one matching the given information (e.g., use $1−2sin²θ$ if only $\sinθ$ is known).
When solving trig equations over an interval, forgetting to check BOTH quadrants where a function is positive/negative loses half the solutions.
$sin²θ+cos²θ=1$ is an identity (true for ALL $θ$) — don't confuse it with an equation to 'solve for $θ$'.

units.name: Analytic Trigonometry & Applications

concepts.intro: For any triangle (not just right triangles) with sides a,b,c opposite angles A,B,C: a/sinA $=$ b/sinB $=$ c/sinC. Used when you know an angle-side opposite pair.
b: Use when given: AAS, ASA, or SSA (the 'ambiguous case')
Set up as a proportion and cross-multiply to solve for the unknown side or angle
Ambiguous case (SSA): given two sides and a non-included angle, there may be 0, 1, or 2 valid triangles — check by comparing the given side to $h=b·sinA$
Sum of angles in any triangle $=$ 180°, so the third angle is always found by subtraction once two are known

concepts.intro: Generalizes the Pythagorean theorem to any triangle: $c²=a²+b²−2ab·cosC$. Used when you know SAS or SSS.
b: Use when given: SAS (two sides and the included angle) or SSS (three sides, no angles)
Solving for a side (SAS): $c²=a²+b²−2ab·cos$ C, then take the square root
Solving for an angle (SSS): rearrange to cos $C=(a²+b²−c²)/(2ab$), then take cos⁻¹
If cos C comes out negative, the angle C is obtuse (>90°) — this is a normal, valid result

concepts.intro: Combine the Law of Sines, Law of Cosines, and area formulas to fully solve (find all sides and angles of) any triangle.
b: SSS or SAS → start with Law of Cosines; AAS/ASA/SSA → start with Law of Sines
Once one angle is found via Law of Cosines, use Law of Sines for the rest (often easier algebra)
Area of any triangle given SAS: $Area=(1/2)ab·sinC$ (works without needing the height)
Heron's formula (SSS, no angles needed): $s=(a+b+c)/2, Area=√[s(s−a)(s−b)(s−c)]$

concepts.intro: Inverse trig functions 'undo' trig functions but must have RESTRICTED ranges to be true functions (since sin, cos, tan are not one-to-one).
b: sin⁻¹x (arcsin): domain [−1,1], range $[−π/2,π/2]$ (QI and QIV)
cos⁻¹x (arccos): domain [−1,1], range $[0,π]$ (QI and QII)
tan⁻¹x (arctan): domain all reals, range ($−π/2,π/2$)
$sin⁻¹(\sinθ)=θ$ only if $θ$ is already in $[−π/2,π/2]$; otherwise find the equivalent angle in range
Example: $sin⁻¹(1/2)=π/6$ (30°) — the answer must be in $[−π/2,π/2]$, so 150° is NOT the output even though $sin150°=1/2$ too
Used to solve for an unknown ANGLE once a trig ratio is known (e.g., in right-triangle applications: angle of elevation/depression)

traps: Law of Sines' SSA case is 'ambiguous' — always check whether 0, 1, or 2 triangles are possible before finalizing an answer.
In Law of Cosines, cos C can be negative — that just means C is obtuse; don't discard the result.
Inverse trig functions return only ONE angle in a restricted range — $sin⁻¹(1/2)=30°$ only, even though 150° also has sine 1/2.
$Area=(1/2)ab$ sinC requires the INCLUDED angle C (between sides a and b), not just any angle.

units.name: Systems & Matrices

concepts.intro: A system of equations has a solution where all equations are simultaneously true — geometrically, where the graphs intersect.
b: Substitution: solve one equation for one variable, substitute into the other equation(s)
Elimination: multiply equations by constants so one variable's coefficients are opposites, then add the equations
Example (elimination): $2x+3y=7$ and $4x−3y=11$ → add directly: $6x=18$ → $x=3$, then $y=1/3(7−6)=1/3$
A system with NO solution: equations simplify to a false statement (e.g., $0=5$) — lines are parallel
A system with INFINITE solutions: equations simplify to a true statement (e.g., $0=0$) — lines coincide
For 3-variable systems, eliminate one variable at a time to reduce to a 2-variable system

concepts.intro: A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers. Its dimensions are given as rows × columns.
b: A matrix with m rows and n columns is an m×n matrix
Two matrices are equal only if they have the same dimensions AND every corresponding entry is equal
A matrix can represent a system of equations as an augmented matrix (coefficients | constants)
Row operations (swap rows, multiply a row by a nonzero constant, add a multiple of one row to another) don't change the system's solution — basis of row-reduction/Gaussian elimination
The identity matrix I (1's on the diagonal, 0's elsewhere) acts like the number 1 in matrix multiplication: $AI=IA=A$

concepts.intro: Addition/subtraction require matching dimensions; multiplication has its own rule based on rows and columns.
b: Add/subtract matrices by adding/subtracting corresponding entries — matrices MUST be the same dimensions
Scalar multiplication: multiply every entry by the scalar
Matrix multiplication AB is defined only if the number of COLUMNS of A equals the number of ROWS of B
Result dimensions: if A is m×n and B is n×p, then AB is m×p
Entry (row i, col j) of AB $=$ dot product of row i of A with column j of B
Matrix multiplication is NOT commutative in general: AB ≠ BA

concepts.intro: The determinant is a single number computed from a square matrix that reveals whether it has an inverse.
b: 2×2 matrix [[a,b],[c,d]]: determinant $=$ ad−bc
A matrix has an inverse iff its determinant ≠ 0 (a matrix with $det=0$ is called 'singular')
3×3 determinant via cofactor expansion along the top row: expand and use the checkerboard sign pattern (+,−,+)
The inverse of a 2×2 matrix [[a,b],[c,d]] is (1/det)·[[d,−b],[−c,a]]

concepts.intro: Cramer's Rule solves a system of linear equations using determinants, without row-reducing.
b: For $ax+by=e, cx+dy=f: x=Dx/D, y=Dy/D$, where D is the coefficient matrix's determinant
$D=det([[a,b],[c,d]]); Dx=det([[e,b],[f,d]]$) (replace the x-column with constants); $Dy=det([[a,e],[c,f]]$) (replace the y-column)
If $D=0$, Cramer's Rule fails — the system either has no solution or infinitely many (cannot be determined by Cramer's Rule alone)

traps: Matrix multiplication AB requires columns of A $=$ rows of B — mismatched dimensions mean the product doesn't exist.
AB ≠ BA in general for matrices — order matters, unlike ordinary number multiplication.
If a system's determinant $D=0$, Cramer's Rule cannot give a unique solution — don't divide by zero.
$det=ad−bc$ for a 2×2 matrix [[a,b],[c,d]] — a common error is bc−ad (sign flipped) or ac−bd (wrong entries).

units.name: Sequences, Series & Conics

concepts.intro: An arithmetic sequence has a CONSTANT difference d between consecutive terms.
b: Explicit (nth term) formula: $aₙ=a₁+(n−1)d$
d $=$ common difference $=$ aₙ − aₙ₋₁ (any term minus the one before it)
Recursive form: $aₙ=aₙ₋₁+d$, with a₁ given
To find d given two non-consecutive terms: $d=(aₙ−aₘ)/(n−m$)

concepts.intro: A geometric sequence has a CONSTANT ratio r between consecutive terms.
b: Explicit (nth term) formula: $aₙ=a₁·r^(n−1$)
r $=$ common ratio $=$ aₙ/aₙ₋₁ (any term divided by the one before it)
If |r|<1, terms shrink toward 0 (e.g., 8,4,2,1,0.5,...); if |r|>1, terms grow without bound
Recursive form: $aₙ=r·aₙ₋₁$, with a₁ given

concepts.intro: A series is the SUM of a sequence's terms. Sigma notation $Σ$ compactly represents these sums.
b: Sigma notation: $Σ(from k=1$ to n) f(k) means add f(1)+f(2)+...+f(n)
Arithmetic series sum: $Sₙ=n(a₁+aₙ)/2 =$ n[2a₁+(n−1)d]/2
Finite geometric series sum: $Sₙ=a₁(1−rⁿ)/(1−r$), for r≠1
Infinite geometric series sum (converges only if |r|<1): $S=a₁/(1−r$)

concepts.intro: A conic section formed by slicing a cone parallel to its side; the set of points equidistant from a focus and a directrix.
b: Vertex form (vertex at origin), opens up/down: $x²=4py (p=distance$ from vertex to focus, and to directrix)
Opens left/right: $y²=4px$
If p>0: opens up (or right); if p<0: opens down (or left)
Focus is INSIDE the curve at distance |p| from vertex; directrix is a line OUTSIDE at distance |p| on the opposite side
Example: $x²=8y$ → $4p=8$ → $p=2$ → focus at (0,2), directrix $y=−2$
General vertex-form parabola (vertex (h,k)): ($x−h)²=4p(y−k$) or ($y−k)²=4p(x−h$)

concepts.intro: Both are centered conics defined by a and b (semi-axes); an ellipse is a 'squashed circle', a hyperbola has two separate branches.
b: Ellipse standard form centered at origin: $x²/a²+y²/b²=1$, where a is the semi-major axis, b the semi-minor axis (a>b)
Ellipse foci lie on the major axis at distance c from center, where $c²=a²−b²$
Hyperbola standard form (opens left/right): $x²/a²−y²/b²=1$; (opens up/down): $y²/a²−x²/b²=1$
Hyperbola foci satisfy $c²=a²+b²$ (note the PLUS sign, unlike the ellipse)
Hyperbolas have asymptotes $y=±(b/a)x$ (for the $x²/a²−y²/b²=1$ form) that the branches approach but never touch
Example: $x²/25+y²/9=1$ is an ellipse with $a=5,b=3$ → $c²=25−9=16$ → $c=4$, foci at (±4,0)

traps: An arithmetic sequence has a constant DIFFERENCE; a geometric sequence has a constant RATIO — don't mix up which formula to use.
Infinite geometric series only converge (have a finite sum) when |r|<1 — if |r|≥1 the sum diverges (no formula applies).
Ellipse foci use $c²=a²−b²$ (minus); hyperbola foci use $c²=a²+b²$ (plus) — swapping these signs gives the wrong foci.
In $x²=4py$, the coefficient of the squared term is 4p, not p — solve for p by dividing by 4, don't forget that step.

units.name: Limits & Intro to Calculus Concepts

concepts.l: The intuitive idea of a limit
concepts.intro: lim(x→a) $f(x)=L$ means f(x) gets arbitrarily close to L as x gets arbitrarily close to a (from both sides), regardless of the actual value f(a) (which may not even exist).
b: A limit describes the function's BEHAVIOR NEAR a point, not necessarily the value AT that point
Two-sided limit exists only if the left-hand limit and right-hand limit are EQUAL: $lim(x→a⁻)f(x)=lim(x→a⁺)f(x$)
Notation: lim(x→a⁻) means approaching from the left (values less than a); lim(x→a⁺) means approaching from the right
A limit can exist at a point even if the function is undefined there (e.g., a hole in the graph)
A limit fails to exist if the function jumps (left/right limits differ), oscillates infinitely, or increases/decreases without bound near a

concepts.intro: Without algebra, limits can be estimated by reading a graph or by plugging in values approaching a from both sides.
b: Graphically: trace the curve from both sides toward $x=a$ and see what y-value it approaches (ignore any open/closed dot exactly at $x=a$)
Numerically: build a table of x-values very close to a (e.g., a−0.1, a−0.01, a+0.01, a+0.1) and see what f(x) approaches
Example: lim(x→2) (x²−4)/(x−2) — direct substitution gives 0/0 (indeterminate), but the table shows values approaching 4
Algebraically confirm: ($x²−4)/(x−2)=(x−2)(x+2)/(x−2)=x+2$ (for x≠2) → limit as x→2 is $2+2=4$
Direct substitution works to evaluate a limit whenever the function is continuous at that point (most polynomials, and rational functions where the denominator isn't 0)

concepts.intro: The average rate of change of f over [a,b] is the slope of the secant line connecting (a,f(a)) and (b,f(b)) — identical in form to the difference quotient.
b: Average rate of change $=$ [f(b)−f(a)] / (b−a)
This is exactly a SLOPE calculation — same formula as (y₂−y₁)/(x₂−x₁)
Example: $f(x)=x²$, find average rate of change on [1,4]: $[f(4)−f(1)]/(4−1)=(16−1)/3=5$
As the interval [a,b] shrinks (b→a), the average rate of change approaches the INSTANTANEOUS rate of change at $x=a$ — this is the core idea that leads to the derivative
Units matter in applications: e.g., average velocity $=$ change in position / change in time

concepts.l: Introduction to derivatives as slope of the tangent line
concepts.intro: The derivative f'(a) is the instantaneous rate of change of f at $x=a$ — the slope of the line TANGENT to the curve at that single point, defined as a limit of average rates of change (secant slopes) as the interval shrinks to zero.
b: Definition: $f'(a)=lim(h→0$) [f(a+h)−f(a)]/h — the limit of the difference quotient as h→0
This is the limiting slope of secant lines through (a,f(a)) and (a+h,f(a+h)) as h shrinks toward 0
Geometrically: the tangent line touches the curve at exactly one point (locally) and matches its instantaneous direction there
Example: for $f(x)=x², f'(a)=lim(h→0$) [(a+h)²−a²]/h $=$ lim(h→0) [2ah+h²]/h $= lim(h→0)(2a+h)=2a$ — so the slope of the tangent to $y=x²$ at any point a is 2a
This 'slope of the tangent line' interpretation is the geometric heart of every derivative computed in calculus

traps: A limit describes behavior NEAR a point — f(a) itself can be undefined, different from the limit, or equal to it; all three are possible.
Direct substitution giving 0/0 does NOT mean the limit doesn't exist — it means you must factor/simplify first (indeterminate form).
A two-sided limit only exists if the LEFT and RIGHT limits are equal — a jump discontinuity means the limit does not exist even if both one-sided limits exist.
Average rate of change is a SECANT slope over an interval; the derivative is the limiting TANGENT slope at a single point — don't conflate the two.

quiz.q: If $f(x)=2x²−3x+1$, find f(3).
If $f(x)=x+2$ and $g(x)=x²$, find (f∘g)(3).
If $f(x)=x+2$ and $g(x)=x²$, find (g∘f)(3).
quiz.e: ($g∘f)(3)=g(f(3))=g(5)=25$. Composition order matters — this differs from (f∘g)(3).

quiz.q: What is the domain of $f(x)=1/(x−5)?$
quiz.e: The denominator cannot equal 0, so x≠5 is excluded.

quiz.q: What is the domain of $f(x)=√(x−4)?$
quiz.e: The radicand must be ≥0 for a real, even-root output: x−4≥0 → x≥4.

quiz.q: Which test determines whether a graph represents a function?
quiz.e: The Vertical Line Test: if any vertical line crosses the graph more than once, it is not a function.

quiz.q: The graph of $y=(x−3)²+5$ is the graph of $y=x²$ shifted:
quiz.e: (x−h) shifts right h units ($h=3$); +k shifts up k units ($k=5$).

quiz.q: The graph of $y=f(x+4$) is obtained from $y=f(x$) by shifting:
quiz.e: f(x+h) shifts LEFT h units — opposite of the sign inside the parentheses.

quiz.q: Which best describes the transformation from $y=x²$ to $y=3x²?$
quiz.e: Multiplying the whole function by a>1 (outside) vertically stretches the graph.

quiz.q: Which function is even?
quiz.e: $f(−x)=(−x)²+3=x²+3=f(x$), so it's even. It's symmetric about the y-axis.

quiz.q: Which function is odd?
quiz.e: $f(−x)=(−x)³−(−x)=−x³+x=−(x³−x)=−f(x$), so it's odd.

quiz.q: Given $f(x)={2x+1$ if x<3; x²−2 if x≥3}, find f(3).
quiz.e: Since 3≥3, use the second rule: $f(3)=3²−2=7$.

quiz.q: Given $f(x)={2x+1$ if x<3; x²−2 if x≥3}, find f(1).
quiz.e: Since 1<3, use the first rule: $f(1)=2(1)+1=3$.

quiz.q: What is the range of $f(x)=−x²+4$ (a downward parabola with vertex (0,4))?
quiz.e: The parabola opens downward with maximum value 4 at the vertex, so the range is y≤4.

quiz.q: The difference quotient [f(x+h)−f(x)]/h for $f(x)=x²$ simplifies to:
quiz.e: $[(x+h)²−x²]/h=[2xh+h²]/h=2x+h$.

quiz.q: Which transformation reflects $y=f(x$) over the x-axis?
quiz.e: −f(x) negates every output (y-value), flipping the graph over the x-axis. f(−x) reflects over the y-axis instead.

quiz.q: What is the end behavior of $f(x)=−3x⁴+2x−1?$
quiz.e: Even degree (4) with negative leading coefficient → falls on both ends.

quiz.q: What is the end behavior of $f(x)=2x⁵−x²+3?$
quiz.e: Odd degree (5) with positive leading coefficient → falls left, rises right.

quiz.q: Find the zeros of $f(x)=x²−4x−5$.
For $f(x)=(x−2)²(x+3$), what is the behavior at $x=2?$
quiz.e: The factor (x−2) has multiplicity 2 (even) → the graph touches and turns back at $x=2$.

quiz.q: Which are the possible rational roots of $2x³+x²−13x+6=0$ given by the Rational Root Theorem, considering $constant=6$ and leading $coefficient=2?$
quiz.e: Candidates $=$ ±(factors of 6)/(factors of 2) $=$ ±1,2,3,6,1/2,3/2.

quiz.q: Using synthetic division, divide x³−6x²+11x−6 by (x−1). What is the remainder?
quiz.e: Synthetic division with root 1: 1,−6,11,−6 → bring down 1, $1(1)−6=−5, −5(1)+11=6, 6(1)−6=0$. Remainder is 0, so $x=1$ is a root.

quiz.q: What is the vertical asymptote of $f(x)=(x+1)/(x−4)?$
quiz.e: Set the denominator to 0: $x−4=0$ → $x=4$. The numerator isn't zero there, so it's a true vertical asymptote.

quiz.q: What is the horizontal asymptote of $f(x)=(2x²+5)/(x²−9)?$
quiz.e: Degrees are equal (both 2), so HA $=$ ratio of leading coefficients $=$ 2/1 $=$ 2.

quiz.q: What is the horizontal asymptote of $f(x)=(3x+1)/(x²−4)?$
quiz.e: Numerator degree (1) is less than denominator degree (2), so HA is $y=0$.

quiz.q: For $f(x)=(x²+3x)/(x²−9$), where is there a HOLE (not an asymptote)?
quiz.e: $f(x)=x(x+3)/[(x−3)(x+3)]$. The (x+3) factor cancels, creating a hole at $x=−3. x=3$ remains a vertical asymptote.

quiz.q: Does $f(x)=(x²+1)/(x−2$) have a horizontal or slant asymptote?
quiz.e: Numerator degree (2) is exactly one more than denominator degree (1) → a slant asymptote exists, found by long division.
A fraction equals 0 only when its numerator is 0 (and denominator isn't): $x−3=0$ → $x=3$.

quiz.q: Solve $3/(x−1)=6/(x+2$) for x.
quiz.e: Cross-multiply: $3(x+2)=6(x−1$) → $3x+6=6x−6$ → $12=3x$ → $x=4$. Check: neither denominator is 0.

quiz.q: Which factorization is correct for x³−8?
quiz.e: Difference of cubes: $a³−b³=(a−b)(a²+ab+b²$), with $a=x,b=2$: (x−2)(x²+2x+4).

quiz.q: Solve the rational inequality (x−1)/(x+2)≥0.
quiz.e: Critical values $x=−2$ (excluded, undefined) and $x=1$ (included, zero). Testing intervals shows the expression is ≥0 for x<−2 or x≥1.

quiz.q: A polynomial of degree 4 can have at most how many real zeros (counting multiplicity)?
quiz.e: A degree-n polynomial has at most n real zeros, counting multiplicity — degree 4 → at most 4.

quiz.e: $cotθ=\cosθ/\sinθ$, so $\sinθ·(\cosθ/\sinθ)=\cosθ$.

quiz.q: Which identity is used to derive $1+cot²θ=csc²θ?$
quiz.e: Dividing every term of $sin²θ+cos²θ=1$ by $sin²θ$ gives $1+cot²θ=csc²θ$.

quiz.q: Solve $\cos(2θ)=\cosθ$ for $θ$ in $[0,2π$) using $\cos(2θ)=2cos²θ−1: 2cos²θ−\cosθ−1=0$.
What is $sec²θ$ − $tan²θ$ equal to for all $θ?$
quiz.e: From $1+tan²θ=sec²θ$, rearranged: $sec²θ−tan²θ=1$ for all $θ$.

quiz.q: Find cos(15°) using cos(45°−30°).
In a triangle, $A=40°, a=15, B=60°$. Find b using the Law of Sines.
In a triangle, $a=8, b=10, C=50°$. Find c using the Law of Cosines.
In a triangle, $a=5, b=7, c=10$. Find angle C using the Law of Cosines.
Find the area of a triangle with $a=6, b=9$, and included angle $C=30°$.
Use Heron's formula to find the area of a triangle with sides $a=5, b=6, c=7 (s=9$).
Which case requires starting with the Law of Cosines rather than the Law of Sines?
quiz.e: With SSS, no angle is known, so Law of Sines (which needs an angle-side pair) can't start the problem — Law of Cosines is needed first.

quiz.q: What is sin⁻¹(1/2)?
quiz.e: sin⁻¹ returns only values in [−90°,90°]. Even though $sin150°=1/2$ too, only 30° is in the restricted range.

quiz.q: What is cos⁻¹(−1/2)?
quiz.e: cos⁻¹ has range [0°,180°]. $\cos(120°)=−1/2$ and 120° is within that range.

quiz.q: What is the range of $y=tan⁻¹(x)?$
quiz.e: arctan's range is the open interval ($−π/2,π/2$), i.e., (−90°,90°), since tangent has vertical asymptotes there.

quiz.q: In triangle solving with SSA, given $a=7, b=10, A=40°$, compute $h=b·sinA$ to test the ambiguous case.
quiz.e: $h=b·sinA=10·sin40°≈10(0.643)≈6.43$. Since $a=7>h$, and a<b, there are two possible triangles.

quiz.q: A triangle has $a=8, b=8, c=8$ (equilateral). What is angle A?
quiz.e: An equilateral triangle has all angles equal, and they must sum to 180°, so each is 60°.

quiz.q: Find angle B in a triangle where $A=35°, C=75°$.
Which formula finds a triangle's area when only the three sides (SSS) are known?
quiz.e: Heron's formula computes area directly from the three side lengths without needing any angle.

quiz.q: If cosC turns out to be negative when applying the Law of Cosines, what does this mean?
quiz.e: A negative cosine value corresponds to an angle between 90° and 180° — this is a valid, expected result.

quiz.q: Evaluate tan⁻¹(1).
quiz.e: $\tan(45°)=1$, and 45° lies within arctan's range of (−90°,90°).

quiz.q: A surveyor measures two sides of a triangular lot as 120 ft and 150 ft with an included angle of 65°. Find the area.
Solve the system: $2x+3y=7$ and $4x−3y=11$.
quiz.e: Add the equations: $6x=18$ → $x=3$. Substitute: $2(3)+3y=7$ → $3y=1$ → $y=1/3$.

quiz.q: Solve the system: $x+y=5$ and $x−y=1$.
Which describes a system with no solution?
o: Elimination leads to a false statement like $0=5$
Elimination leads to a true statement like $0=0$
Elimination gives a unique x and y
quiz.e: A false numerical statement means the equations are contradictory — parallel lines that never intersect.

quiz.q: Which describes a system with infinitely many solutions?
o: Elimination leads to a true statement like $0=0$
Elimination leads to a false statement like $0=5$
The system has a unique solution
quiz.e: A true statement with no variables means the two equations represent the same line.

quiz.q: A matrix has 3 rows and 5 columns. What are its dimensions?
quiz.e: Matrix dimensions are given as rows × columns: 3×5.

quiz.q: For matrix multiplication AB to be defined, what must be true?
o: Columns of A $=$ Rows of B
Rows of A $=$ Rows of B
Columns of A $=$ Columns of B
A and B must have the same dimensions
quiz.e: Matrix multiplication AB requires the number of columns in A to equal the number of rows in B.

quiz.q: If A is 2×3 and B is 3×4, what are the dimensions of AB?
quiz.e: The product takes the outer dimensions: rows of A (2) × columns of B (4) $=$ 2×4.

quiz.q: Find the determinant of [[2,3],[1,4]].
Find the determinant of [[5,2],[3,1]].
A matrix has determinant 0. What does this mean?
o: The matrix is singular (has no inverse)
The matrix equals the identity matrix
The matrix is a zero matrix
quiz.e: A determinant of 0 means the matrix is 'singular' and has no inverse.

quiz.q: Use Cramer's Rule to solve $2x+y=5, x−3y=−8$. What is D (the coefficient determinant)?
Using the system $2x+y=5, x−3y=−8 (D=−7$), find x using Cramer's Rule, where $Dx=det([[5,1],[−8,−3]]$).
Find the inverse of [[2,1],[1,1]].
If Cramer's Rule gives $D=0$ for a system, what can be concluded?
o: The system has no unique solution — either none or infinitely many
The system definitely has infinitely many solutions
The system definitely has no solution
quiz.e: $D=0$ means Cramer's Rule cannot determine a unique solution — further analysis (or another method) is needed to tell no-solution from infinite-solutions.

quiz.q: Is matrix multiplication commutative ($AB=BA$) in general?
quiz.e: Matrix multiplication is generally NOT commutative — AB and BA can even have different dimensions or different values.

quiz.q: What is the identity matrix's role in matrix multiplication?
o: It always produces the zero matrix
It reverses the sign of every entry
quiz.e: The identity matrix I acts as the multiplicative identity: multiplying any compatible matrix A by I returns A unchanged.

quiz.q: Find the 10th term of the arithmetic sequence 5,9,13,17,...
Find the 8th term of the geometric sequence 3,6,12,24,...
Find the sum of the first 20 terms of the arithmetic sequence 4,7,10,...
Find the sum of the infinite geometric series 1+1/2+1/4+1/8+...
Find the sum of the first 6 terms of the geometric series 2+6+18+54+...
Does the infinite series 3+6+12+24+... have a finite sum?
quiz.e: $r=2$, and infinite geometric series only converge when |r|<1. Since |2|≥1, this series diverges (no finite sum).

quiz.q: Find the common difference of the arithmetic sequence where $a₅=17$ and $a₁₂=45$.
For the parabola $x²=8y$, find the focus.
quiz.e: $x²=4py$ → $4p=8$ → $p=2$. Vertex at origin, opens up, focus at ($0,p)=(0,2$).

quiz.q: For the parabola $x²=8y$, find the directrix.
quiz.e: With $p=2$, the directrix is the horizontal line $y=−p=−2$ (opposite side of vertex from the focus).

quiz.q: For the ellipse $x²/25+y²/9=1$, find the foci.
quiz.e: $a²=25,b²=9$ → $c²=25−9=16$ → $c=4$. Since the larger denominator is under x², foci are on the x-axis: (±4,0).

quiz.q: For the hyperbola $x²/16−y²/9=1$, find c (distance from center to each focus).
quiz.e: For a hyperbola, $c²=a²+b²=16+9=25$ → $c=5$.

quiz.q: What are the asymptotes of the hyperbola $x²/16−y²/9=1?$
quiz.e: For $x²/a²−y²/b²=1$, asymptotes are $y=±(b/a)x =$ ±(3/4)x ($a²=16→a=4, b²=9→b=3$).

quiz.q: Evaluate $Σ(k=1$ to 5) (2k+1).
quiz.e: Terms: $3+5+7+9+11=35$ (an arithmetic series with $a₁=3, d=2, n=5: S=5(3+11)/2=35$).

quiz.q: A geometric sequence has $a₁=100$ and $r=0.5$. What is a₅?
Which conic is $x²/9+y²/25=1?$
o: An ellipse with major axis along the y-axis
An ellipse with major axis along the x-axis
quiz.e: Both terms are added (ellipse) and the larger denominator (25) is under y², so the major axis is vertical.

quiz.q: A ball is dropped from 10 ft and bounces back to 60% of its previous height each time. What is the total distance the ball has fallen for the infinite bounces (sum of all drop heights after the first, i.e., 10(0.6)+10(0.6)²+...)?
quiz.e: This is an infinite geometric series with $a₁=10(0.6)=6, r=0.6: S=6/(1−0.6)=6/0.4=15$ ft.

quiz.q: Evaluate lim(x→3) (x²−9)/(x−3).
quiz.e: Factor: ($x−3)(x+3)/(x−3)=x+3$ for x≠3. As x→3, this approaches $3+3=6$.

quiz.q: Evaluate lim(x→2) (x²+3x−1).
quiz.e: This is a polynomial (continuous everywhere) so use direct substitution: $4+6−1=9$.

quiz.q: If lim(x→2⁻) $f(x)=5$ and lim(x→2⁺) $f(x)=5$, what can be concluded about lim(x→2) f(x)?
quiz.e: Since the left-hand and right-hand limits agree (both 5), the two-sided limit exists and equals 5, regardless of f(2).

quiz.q: If lim(x→1⁻) $f(x)=3$ and lim(x→1⁺) $f(x)=7$, what can be concluded about lim(x→1) f(x)?
quiz.e: The one-sided limits disagree, so the overall (two-sided) limit does not exist there.

quiz.q: Find the average rate of change of $f(x)=x²$ over [1,4].
Find the average rate of change of $f(x)=2x²+1$ over [0,3].
What does the average rate of change of a function over [a,b] represent geometrically?
o: The slope of the secant line through (a,f(a)) and (b,f(b))
The slope of the tangent line at $x=a$
quiz.e: Average rate of change is exactly the slope formula (y₂−y₁)/(x₂−x₁), which is the secant line's slope.

quiz.q: Using $f(x)=x²$, find f'(a) via the definition $f'(a)=lim(h→0)[f(a+h)−f(a)]/h$.
quiz.e: $[(a+h)²−a²]/h=[2ah+h²]/h=2a+h$ → as h→0, this approaches 2a.

quiz.q: What does f'(a) represent geometrically?
o: The slope of the tangent line to f at $x=a$
The slope of the secant line over an interval
The average value of f near a
quiz.e: The derivative f'(a) is defined as the limiting slope of secant lines as h→0, which is exactly the slope of the tangent line at $x=a$.

quiz.q: For $f(x)=x²+2x$, find f'(a) using the limit definition.
quiz.e: $[(a+h)²+2(a+h)−(a²+2a)]/h=[2ah+h²+2h]/h=2a+h+2$ → as h→0, this approaches 2a+2.

quiz.q: A function f is continuous at $x=a$. How can lim(x→a) f(x) be evaluated?
o: It cannot be found without a table
quiz.e: If f is continuous at a, then $lim(x→a)f(x)=f(a$), so plugging in a directly gives the limit.

quiz.q: Evaluate lim(x→0) (sin x)/x using a table of values approaching 0 (a well-known result).
quiz.e: This classic limit approaches 1 as x→0 from both sides, even though direct substitution gives the indeterminate form 0/0.

quiz.q: A car travels so that its position is $s(t)=t²+3t$ (meters, seconds). Find the average velocity over [2,5].
Which situation describes a limit that does NOT exist as x→a?
o: The left and right limits approach different values
f(a) is undefined but both one-sided limits agree
The function is continuous at a
quiz.e: When the left-hand and right-hand limits disagree, no single limiting value exists — this is the defining condition for the limit failing to exist.

quiz.q: Given $f(x)=(x²−1)/(x−1$) for x≠1, what is lim(x→1) f(x)?
quiz.e: Factor: ($x−1)(x+1)/(x−1)=x+1$ for x≠1. As x→1, this approaches $1+1=2$ (even though f(1) itself is undefined — a hole).

quiz.q: What is the relationship between average rate of change and the derivative as the interval [a,b] shrinks (b→a)?
o: Average rate of change approaches the instantaneous rate of change (the derivative) at a
They are always equal for any interval
quiz.e: As the interval shrinks to a single point, the secant slope (average rate) approaches the tangent slope (derivative) — this limiting process is the foundation of differential calculus.

PART_A.q: Which conclusion resulted directly from the gold foil experiment?
o: Electrons in an atom are negatively charged
Atoms contain a small, dense nucleus
Electrons in an atom are in shells that have different energies
PART_A.e: Rutherford's gold foil experiment: most α particles passed through (empty space); few deflected → small dense positive nucleus.

PART_A.q: What is the number of electrons in a neutral atom with 37 protons and 49 neutrons?
PART_A.e: Neutral atom: electrons = protons = 37.

PART_A.q: Which statement describes the mass of an electron?
o: An electron has the same mass as a proton
An electron has the same mass as a neutron
An electron has much less mass than a proton
An electron has much more mass than a neutron
PART_A.e: Electron mass ≈ 1/1836 of a proton. Much less mass than either proton or neutron.

PART_A.q: In the wave-mechanical model of the atom, electrons are located in regions called
PART_A.e: Wave-mechanical model: electrons occupy orbitals — regions of probability, not fixed paths.

PART_A.q: At STP, a sample of potassium can be differentiated from a sample of rubidium based on
PART_A.e: Both are solid metals at STP (same phase). Density is an intensive physical property that differs between the two.

PART_A.q: Which statement describes a chemical property of chlorine?
o: Chlorine has an atomic radius of 100. pm
Chlorine reacts with sodium to form a salt
Chlorine has a melting point of 172 K
Chlorine is a green-yellow gas at STP
PART_A.e: A chemical property describes how a substance reacts. Reacting with Na to form NaCl is a chemical property. Radius, MP, and color/phase are physical properties.

PART_A.q: Oxygen gas, O₂(g), and ozone gas, O₃(g), are two forms of the element oxygen. These two forms of oxygen have
o: the same molecular structures and the same properties
the same molecular structures and different properties
different molecular structures and the same properties
different molecular structures and different properties
PART_A.e: O₂ and O₃ are allotropes — same element, different molecular structures → different chemical and physical properties.

PART_A.q: Which phrase describes two or more elements chemically combined?
o: a mixture with a fixed proportion of elements
a mixture with variable proportions of elements
a compound with a fixed proportion of elements
a compound with variable proportions of elements
PART_A.e: A compound is formed when two or more elements are chemically combined in fixed (definite) proportions.

PART_A.q: Which formula is an empirical formula?
PART_A.e: N₂O₅: simplest ratio is already N₂O₅ (cannot be reduced). N₂O₄ reduces to NO₂; N₂F₂ reduces to NF; N₂H₄ reduces to NH₂.

PART_A.q: Which terms represent two different categories of compounds?
PART_A.e: Ionic and molecular (covalent) are the two main categories of compounds. 'Covalent' and 'molecular' are the same category; 'electrical' is not a compound category.

PART_A.q: Which element has molecules that each contain a multiple covalent bond?
PART_A.e: O₂ contains a double bond (O=O). H₂, Br₂, I₂ each contain only single bonds.

PART_A.q: Which formula represents an asymmetrical (polar) molecule?
PART_A.e: HCl has two different atoms → unequal EN → polar bond AND linear asymmetric shape → polar molecule. CO₂ is linear symmetric; Cl₂ is nonpolar; CH₄ is tetrahedral symmetric.

PART_A.q: Which changes in charge and radius occur when an atom gains one electron?
o: A negative ion forms with a radius smaller than the atom
A negative ion forms with a radius larger than the atom
A positive ion forms with a radius smaller than the atom
A positive ion forms with a radius larger than the atom
PART_A.e: Gaining an electron: more electrons repel each other → larger radius; net negative charge → anion.

PART_A.q: Given: N + N → N₂. What occurs during this reaction?
o: Energy is absorbed as bonds are broken
Energy is absorbed as bonds are formed
Energy is released as bonds are broken
Energy is released as bonds are formed
PART_A.e: Forming bonds always releases energy (exothermic). N≡N triple bond formation releases energy → products side.

PART_A.q: Which compound has both ionic and covalent bonds?
PART_A.e: KClO₂ contains K⁺ and ClO₂⁻ (ionic bond between them) AND covalent Cl−O bonds inside the polyatomic ion. CaCl₂, Li₂S, MnO₂ have no polyatomic ions.

PART_A.q: Which substance cannot be broken down by a chemical change?
PART_A.e: Fe is an element — cannot be broken down chemically. All the others are compounds that can be decomposed.

PART_A.q: According to the kinetic molecular theory, the particles of an ideal gas have
o: collisions that do not transfer energy
large volumes compared to the distances between them
PART_A.e: KMT: gas particles move in constant, random, straight-line motion. Collisions are elastic (do transfer energy); no attractive forces; particle volume is negligible.

PART_A.q: In order for a chemical reaction to occur, colliding particles must have proper orientation and proper
PART_A.e: Collision theory requires: (1) collision, (2) proper orientation, AND (3) sufficient energy (≥ Ea).

PART_A.q: At STP, which sample of gas has the same number of atoms as 4.0 liters of Ne gas?
PART_A.e: Avogadro's Law: equal volumes at same T and P = equal molecules. Ne and Xe are both monatomic (1 atom/molecule). 4.0 L Xe = 4.0 L Ne in atom count.

PART_A.q: Based on Table I, the dissolving of which compound is an exothermic process at 298 K and 101.3 kPa?
PART_A.e: Table I: NaOH dissolving has a negative ΔH → exothermic (solution warms). KNO₃, NH₄Cl, NH₄NO₃ have positive ΔH → endothermic.

PART_A.q: Which expression represents the heat of reaction for a chemical change in terms of potential energy, PE?
o: PE of products × PE of reactants
PE of products ÷ PE of reactants
PE of products + PE of reactants
PE of products − PE of reactants
PART_A.e: ΔH = H_products − H_reactants (subtraction). Positive = endothermic; negative = exothermic.

PART_A.q: Which phrase describes how a catalyst increases the rate of a chemical reaction?
o: increases the potential energy of the reactants
increases the activation energy of the reaction
PART_A.e: A catalyst provides an alternate reaction pathway with a LOWER activation energy → more collisions succeed → faster rate.

PART_A.q: At standard pressure, which 5.0-gram sample of xenon has the greatest entropy?
PART_A.e: Entropy: gas > liquid > solid. Xe(g) at 165 K is in the gas state → most disordered → greatest entropy.

PART_A.q: Systems in nature tend to undergo changes that result in
PART_A.e: Natural processes favor lower energy (exothermic) AND greater disorder (higher entropy). ΔG = ΔH − TΔS is negative when both conditions are met.

PART_A.q: Which compound is a member of the homologous series with general formula CₙH₂ₙ?
PART_A.e: CₙH₂ₙ = alkenes. n=3: C₃H₆ ✓. C₂H₂ = alkyne (CₙH₂ₙ₋₂); C₄H₁₀ = alkane (CₙH₂ₙ₊₂); C₅H₈ doesn't fit simply.

PART_A.q: Which term identifies a reaction that produces an alcohol?
PART_A.e: Fermentation: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂. Glucose → ethanol (an alcohol) using yeast.

PART_A.q: Which statement describes a substance that is an electrolyte?
o: The substance conducts an electric current and cannot dissolve in water
The substance cannot conduct an electric current and cannot dissolve in water
When the substance dissolves in water, the solution can conduct an electric current
When the substance dissolves in water, the solution cannot conduct an electric current
PART_A.e: An electrolyte dissolves in water to produce ions → solution conducts electricity.

PART_A.q: Which substance is an Arrhenius acid?
PART_A.e: Arrhenius acid: releases H⁺ in water. HNO₃ → H⁺ + NO₃⁻. NH₃ is a base; NaCl is a salt; NaOH is a base.

PART_A.q: A heavy nucleus splits into two lighter nuclei during which process?
PART_A.e: Nuclear fission: heavy nucleus (e.g., U-235) splits into smaller nuclei + neutrons + energy. Not to be confused with chemical decomposition.

PART_A.q: The energy released by nuclear fusion in the Sun results from the conversion of
PART_A.e: E = mc². In fusion, the product nuclei have less mass than the reactants. This mass deficit is converted to enormous energy (Einstein's equation).

PART_B1.q: Which electron configuration represents a lithium atom in an excited state?
PART_B1.e: Li has 3 electrons. Ground state = 2-1. Excited: an electron jumps to a higher shell. 1-1-1 = 3 electrons spread across 3 shells → excited state.

PART_B1.q: Selenium (Se) is in Group 16. How many valence electrons does a ground-state Se atom have?
PART_B1.e: Group 16 elements have 6 valence electrons. Se: [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p⁴ → 6 valence electrons.

PART_B1.q: Which element could be represented by X in the oxide formula X₂O?
PART_B1.e: X₂O: 2 X atoms balance O²⁻ → each X = +1. Group 1 elements have +1 charge. Cs is Group 1.

PART_B1.q: What is the chemical name for the compound PdO?
PART_B1.e: O = −2, so Pd = +2 for neutral compound. Roman numeral II → palladium(II) oxide.

PART_B1.q: CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → 2H₂O(ℓ) + CO₂(g). When 12 g CH₄ reacts with 48 g O₂ to produce 33 g CO₂, how many grams of H₂O are produced?
PART_B1.e: Conservation of mass: 12 + 48 = 60 g total reactants. Products: 33 g CO₂ + x g H₂O = 60 g → x = 27 g H₂O.

PART_B1.q: What is the gram-formula mass of P₂O₅? (P = 31, O = 16)
In the ground state, ions of which two elements each have the same electron configuration as neon?
PART_B1.e: Ne has 10 electrons. Mg²⁺ (loses 2 e⁻: 12−2=10); O²⁻ (gains 2 e⁻: 8+2=10). Both isoelectronic with Ne.

PART_B1.q: Fluorine (F₂) is a diatomic gas at STP. Which particle model diagram correctly represents a sample of fluorine at STP?
o: Pairs of identical atoms, gas phase (spread out)
PART_B1.e: F₂ at STP: diatomic molecules (pairs of identical F atoms) in the gas phase → spread out, paired.

PART_B1.q: Based on Table F, which compound is most soluble in water?
PART_B1.e: Table F: AgNO₃ is listed as soluble (all nitrates are soluble). Ag₂CrO₄, CuCO₃, Cu₃(PO₄)₂ are all insoluble.

PART_B1.q: Which solution has the lowest freezing point?
PART_B1.e: 2.0 M NaCl → 2.0×2 = 4.0 mol particles/L (Na⁺ + Cl⁻). Most particles → greatest FP depression → lowest FP.

PART_B1.q: What is the amount of heat energy required to completely vaporize 12.5 g of H₂O(ℓ) at 373 K? (H_v = 2260 J/g)
PART_B1.e: q = mH_v = 12.5 g × 2260 J/g = 28,250 J ≈ 28,300 J. At 100°C = phase change → use H_v.

PART_B1.q: A 2.0-gram sample of solid iron reacts with 25 mL of 0.10 M HCl(aq). Which conditions produce the fastest reaction rate?
PART_B1.e: Fastest rate: powdered iron (max surface area) at 303 K (higher temperature) → most frequent, highest-energy collisions.

PART_B1.q: Which term describes a sealed 100.-mL flask containing 50. grams of water at 25°C?
PART_B1.e: Sealed flask: evaporation rate = condensation rate → liquid-vapor physical equilibrium. No chemical reaction occurs.

PART_B1.q: For the reaction N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g), a concentration-vs-time graph shows concentrations becoming constant at approximately 50 s. At which time is the system at equilibrium?
PART_B1.e: Equilibrium is reached when all concentration curves become flat and remain constant. The graph levels off at ≈50 s.

PART_B1.q: Given: H₂(g) + I₂(g) + energy ⇌ 2HI(g). When temperature is increased, equilibrium shifts to the
o: right and the concentration of HI(g) decreases
right and the concentration of HI(g) increases
left and the concentration of HI(g) decreases
left and the concentration of HI(g) increases
PART_B1.e: Endothermic (heat is a reactant). Increasing T adds a reactant → shifts RIGHT → more HI produced.

PART_B1.q: A structural formula shows a 6-carbon chain with a CH₃ branch at carbon 3. What is the IUPAC name?
PART_B1.e: Longest chain = 6 carbons (hexane). CH₃ branch on C3 → 3-methylhexane. Number from the end giving the branch the lowest number.

PART_B1.q: What is the oxidation state of chlorine in the compound KClO₃?
In the reversible reaction NH₃(g) + H₂O(ℓ) ⇌ NH₄⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq), the species in the reverse reaction that donates an H⁺ ion is
PART_B1.e: In the reverse reaction: NH₄⁺ → NH₃ + H⁺ (donates a proton) → NH₄⁺ is the Brønsted-Lowry acid in the reverse direction.

PART_B1.q: When the pH value of a solution changes from 4.0 to 7.0, what is the change in the concentration of hydronium ions?
PART_B1.e: pH increases by 3 → [H₃O⁺] decreases by 10³ = 1000×. Higher pH = less acidic = fewer H⁺ ions.

PART_B1.q: A radioactive emission from chromium-51 passes straight through an electric field without deflection. Which type of emission is this?
PART_B1.e: Gamma radiation has no charge and no mass → not deflected by electric fields. Alpha (+2) and beta (−1) and positron (+1) are all deflected.

PART_B2.q: Determine the percent composition by mass of Cu in CuSO₄ (GFM = 160. g/mol). Show your work.
PART_B2.sa:
% Cu = (mass of Cu / GFM of CuSO₄) × 100
= (64 g/mol / 160. g/mol) × 100
= 40.%

Answer: 40.% Cu

PART_B2.q: State, in terms of both protons and neutrons, why an atom of K-39 is an isotope of an atom of K-40.
PART_B2.sa: Both K-39 and K-40 have the same number of protons (19 protons each — same element, potassium), but K-39 has 20 neutrons while K-40 has 21 neutrons. Isotopes have the same proton count but different neutron counts.

PART_B2.q: Compare the energy of an electron in the first shell of a potassium atom to the energy of an electron in the fourth shell of the same atom.
PART_B2.sa: An electron in the first shell has LESS energy than an electron in the fourth shell. Electrons closer to the nucleus (lower shell number) are at lower energy levels. The fourth shell is at a higher energy level than the first shell.

PART_B2.q: Show a numerical setup for calculating the atomic mass of potassium using the isotope data: K-39 (38.964 u, 93.26%), K-40 (39.964 u, 0.01%), K-41 (40.962 u, 6.73%).
Given: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g) + 91.8 kJ. State, in terms of the number of each type of atom, why this equation is balanced.
PART_B2.sa:
The equation is balanced because the number of each type of atom is the same on both sides:
• Nitrogen: 2 atoms on the left (N₂), 2 atoms on the right (2NH₃) ✓
• Hydrogen: 6 atoms on the left (3H₂ = 3×2), 6 atoms on the right (2NH₃ = 2×3) ✓
Mass is conserved.

PART_B2.q: Given: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g) + 91.8 kJ. State evidence from the equation that the reaction is exothermic.
PART_B2.sa: Evidence: The energy term (91.8 kJ) appears on the product side (right side) of the equation. This means energy is released as a product of the reaction → exothermic. Also, ΔH is negative for exothermic reactions.

PART_B2.q: Determine the number of moles of H₂(g) required to react completely with N₂(g) to produce 10.0 moles of NH₃(g). (N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃)
PART_B2.sa:
Mole ratio H₂ : NH₃ = 3 : 2

Moles H₂ = 10.0 mol NH₃ × (3 mol H₂ / 2 mol NH₃)

= 15.0 mol H₂

PART_B2.q: A 320.-mL sample of N₂(g) is at 300. K and 100. kPa. State the number of significant figures in the original temperature.
PART_B2.sa:
300. K — the decimal point after 300 makes all three digits significant.

Answer: 3 significant figures

PART_B2.q: Compare the force of collisions of N₂ gas particles at 300. K to the force of collisions at 450. K.
PART_B2.sa: At 450. K, the force of collisions is GREATER than at 300. K. Higher temperature means particles have greater average kinetic energy and move faster → collide with greater force.

PART_B2.q: State a change in temperature AND a change in pressure that will cause N₂ gas to behave more like an ideal gas.
PART_B2.sa:
Increase the temperature AND decrease the pressure.

Reason: High temperature → particles move faster, spend less time near each other → intermolecular attractions are less significant. Low pressure → particles are farther apart → less interaction. Both conditions reduce deviation from ideal behavior.

PART_B2.q: Determine the volume of N₂ gas when temperature changes to 450. K and pressure changes to 60.0 kPa. (Initial: 320. mL, 300. K, 100. kPa)
PART_B2.sa:
Combined Gas Law: P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂

V₂ = (P₁ × V₁ × T₂) / (T₁ × P₂)
= (100. kPa × 320. mL × 450. K) / (300. K × 60.0 kPa)
= 14,400,000 / 18,000
= 800. mL

PART_C.q: State, in terms of valence electrons, why bromine and iodine have similar chemical properties.
PART_C.sa: Bromine and iodine are both in Group 17 (halogens). Both have 7 valence electrons. Elements with the same number of valence electrons have similar chemical properties because they react in the same way to complete their outermost shell.

PART_C.q: State, in terms of the strength of intermolecular forces, why bromine has a higher boiling point than chlorine at standard pressure.
PART_C.sa: Bromine (Br₂) has stronger intermolecular forces (London dispersion forces) than chlorine (Cl₂). Br₂ has more electrons and greater molar mass → stronger temporary dipoles → stronger LDFs. Stronger IMFs require more energy to overcome → higher boiling point.

PART_C.q: Based on Table S, state the trend in first ionization energy for the four halogen elements (F, Cl, Br, I) as atomic number increases.
PART_C.sa: As atomic number increases (F → Cl → Br → I), the first ionization energy decreases. Going down the group, electrons are farther from the nucleus (more electron shells) → held less tightly → less energy required to remove the outermost electron.

PART_C.q: Based on Table S, state why the tungsten filament does not melt in the operating halogen lightbulb at 3200 K.
PART_C.sa: According to Table S, the melting point of tungsten (W) is 3695 K. Since the operating temperature of the halogen lightbulb (3200 K) is below tungsten's melting point (3695 K), the filament remains solid and does not melt.

PART_C.q: State the element classification of tungsten.
PART_C.sa: Tungsten (W) is classified as a metal (specifically a transition metal, located in Group 6 of the d-block on the periodic table).

PART_C.q: Convert the temperature of the dry towel after 8 minutes (22.0°C) to kelvins.
Determine the amount of heat absorbed when 3.60 grams of water is heated from 22.0°C to 67.0°C. (C_water = 4.18 J/g·K)
State the direction of heat flow between the hot water on the towel (67°C) and the air at room temperature (22°C).
PART_C.sa: Heat flows from the hot water on the towel (higher temperature, 67°C) to the cooler surrounding air (lower temperature, 22°C). Heat always flows from higher temperature to lower temperature.

PART_C.q: State what happens to the potential energy of the water molecules as water evaporates from the wet towels.
PART_C.sa: The potential energy of the water molecules INCREASES as water evaporates. Molecules must overcome the intermolecular attractive forces (hydrogen bonds) to escape the liquid surface. This requires energy input, which is stored as potential energy in the separated molecules.

PART_C.q: State, in terms of experimental design, why the student left one paper towel dry on a beaker.
PART_C.sa: The dry towel serves as the CONTROL in the experiment. It provides a baseline (no evaporation occurring) to compare against the wet towels. Without a control, the student could not determine whether any temperature change was caused by evaporation or by some other variable.

PART_C.q: State the form of energy that is converted to electrical energy in the operating voltaic cell (Ni²⁺ + Zn → Ni + Zn²⁺).
PART_C.sa: Chemical energy is converted to electrical energy. In a voltaic cell, a spontaneous redox reaction releases energy, which is captured as electrical energy (electron flow through the external circuit).

PART_C.q: Identify the electrode that is the anode in the voltaic cell: Ni²⁺(aq) + Zn(s) → Ni(s) + Zn²⁺(aq).
PART_C.sa: The ZINC (Zn) electrode is the anode. In this reaction, Zn is oxidized: Zn(s) → Zn²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻. Oxidation always occurs at the anode.

PART_C.q: Write a balanced half-reaction for what occurs at the nickel electrode in the voltaic cell above.
PART_C.sa:
At the nickel electrode (cathode), Ni²⁺ is reduced:

Ni²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → Ni(s)

(Reduction occurs at the cathode — electrons are gained)

PART_C.q: Identify the negative ion present in the NaOH(aq) solution.
PART_C.sa:
The negative ion in NaOH(aq) is the hydroxide ion: OH⁻

NaOH dissociates completely: NaOH → Na⁺ + OH⁻

PART_C.q: Complete the neutralization: HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) → NaCl(aq) + ___
PART_C.sa:
The missing product is H₂O (water).

Full equation: HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(ℓ)

Acid + Base → Salt + Water (neutralization)

PART_C.q: State the color of methyl orange indicator if added to a sample of NaOH(aq).
PART_C.sa: Methyl orange in NaOH(aq) would be YELLOW. NaOH is a strong base (pH >> 7). According to Table M, methyl orange is yellow in base (pH > 4.4).

PART_C.q: Determine the concentration of HCl(aq) using titration data: 15.0 mL HCl neutralized by 25.2 mL of 0.50 M NaOH.
Based on Table N, state the decay mode of tritium (H-3).
PART_C.sa:
According to Table N, tritium (H-3) undergoes beta-minus (β⁻) decay.

Decay: ³₁H → ⁰₋₁e + ³₂He

A neutron converts to a proton plus a high-speed electron (beta particle).

PART_C.q: Complete the nuclear fusion equation for deuterium + tritium: ²₁H + ³₁H → ___ + ¹₀n
PART_C.sa:
²₁H + ³₁H → ⁴₂He + ¹₀n

Check: Mass numbers: 2+3 = 4+1 = 5 ✓
Atomic numbers: 1+1 = 2+0 = 2 ✓

The missing product is ⁴₂He (helium-4 / alpha particle).

PART_C.q: Based on Table N, determine the fraction of an original sample of tritium (H-3, t½ = 12.31 yr) that remains unchanged after 36.93 years.
PART_C.sa:
Number of half-lives = total time / t½ = 36.93 yr / 12.31 yr = 3 half-lives

Fraction remaining = (½)³ = 1/8

Answer: 1/8 of the original sample remains after 36.93 years.
